title: Lung Cancer & Thoracic Surgery: Screening, Diagnosis, Recovery and Oncologic Emergencies
html:
Lung cancer care connects prevention, timely diagnosis, staging, individualized treatment, and symptom support. The RN must distinguish screening of an asymptomatic person from evaluation of a new symptom, prepare clients for tissue sampling or surgery, recognize respiratory and oncologic complications, and support informed goals of care without assuming every tumor follows the same pathway.

Learning goals

  • Apply current U.S. lung-cancer screening eligibility to an asymptomatic adult.
  • Recognize symptoms and emergencies that require diagnostic evaluation rather than screening.
  • Explain how tissue diagnosis, staging, biomarkers, and functional status guide treatment.
  • Plan safe care before and after bronchoscopy, biopsy, and lung resection.
  • Identify superior vena cava syndrome, spinal cord compression, SIADH, and treatment-related pulmonary toxicity.
  • Use all six clinical-judgment steps and communicate with the client and team.

Screening is not diagnostic evaluation

Smoking is the leading risk factor, but lung cancer can occur in people who have never smoked. Ask about tobacco history, secondhand smoke, radon, occupational exposures, family history, prior radiation, and access to follow-up. Offer smoking-cessation support to all who use tobacco; screening does not replace cessation.

The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force recommends annual low-dose CT (LDCT) for adults aged 50–80 years with at least 20 pack-years of smoking who currently smoke or quit within the past 15 years. One pack-year means an average of one pack per day for one year: one pack daily for 20 years or two packs daily for 10 years both equal 20 pack-years. Screening should stop once a person has not smoked for 15 years or develops a health problem that substantially limits life expectancy or the ability or willingness to have curative lung surgery. Discuss potential benefits, false positives, follow-up procedures, and preferences before screening. Apply the current policy and the person's circumstances, not a memorized number alone.

Screening versus symptoms
LDCT screening is for eligible people without lung-cancer symptoms. New hemoptysis, persistent or changing cough, unexplained weight loss, chest pain, hoarseness, dyspnea, or recurrent pneumonia needs timely clinical evaluation even if the person is ineligible for screening or had a prior negative LDCT.

Recognize concerning patterns

Symptoms can be subtle and overlap with COPD or infection. Document onset, progression, amount of blood in sputum, breathing and oxygenation, pain, weight change, appetite, activity tolerance, smoking and exposure history, and baseline findings. A large-volume bleed, airway compromise, rapidly worsening dyspnea, new neurologic deficit, or hemodynamic instability is an emergency. Do not reassure a symptomatic client solely because a prior screening result was negative.

Diagnosis, staging, and treatment are linked

Chest CT characterizes a suspicious finding; PET/CT and other studies may assess extent. Tissue is usually obtained through bronchoscopy with endobronchial ultrasound, image-guided needle biopsy, or another site-specific approach. The team integrates pathology, stage, molecular and immune biomarkers when appropriate, cardiopulmonary reserve, performance status, and the client's goals. A suspicious image is not by itself a complete diagnosis or treatment plan.

Non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and small-cell lung cancer (SCLC) differ in biology and typical treatment. Selected localized NSCLC may be managed with surgery or radiation; systemic targeted therapy, immunotherapy, chemotherapy, and combined approaches depend on stage and tumor characteristics. SCLC is often more widespread at diagnosis and is usually treated with systemic therapy, sometimes with radiation. Never promise that surgery, a particular drug, or cure is appropriate before staging and specialist review.

Protect clients during bronchoscopy and biopsy

Before the procedure, verify identity, indication, consent process, allergies, anticoagulants and bleeding risk, baseline respiratory status, airway plan, and ordered fasting or sedation instructions. After bronchoscopy with topical anesthetic or sedation, assess airway, oxygenation, vital signs, mental status, swallowing and protective reflexes; do not give oral intake until the approved recovery criteria are met. Monitor for bleeding, bronchospasm, aspiration, and pneumothorax as relevant to the procedure.

After transthoracic needle biopsy, assess for new dyspnea, pleuritic pain, falling saturation, reduced breath sounds, and hemoptysis. A stable client still needs the ordered observation and imaging pathway; an unstable client needs immediate escalation. Report the amount and trend of bleeding rather than labeling all blood-streaked sputum as harmless.

Prepare for thoracic surgery

Resection may remove a wedge, segment, lobe, or entire lung. The amount removed changes remaining pulmonary reserve. Preoperative assessment includes pulmonary function, functional capacity, comorbid disease, nutrition, medication reconciliation, smoking status, baseline oxygenation, and the planned procedure. Teach pain control, supported coughing, deep breathing or prescribed pulmonary exercises, early assisted mobility, and what drains and monitoring may be used. Coordinate expectations with the surgical team and the person's goals.

Postoperative care: breathe, perfuse, mobilize

On return from surgery, assess airway and work of breathing first, then oxygenation, breath sounds, chest movement, hemodynamics, rhythm, consciousness, pain and sedation, incision, drains, and urine output. Trend rather than relying on a single value. Watch for bleeding, atelectasis, pneumonia, air leak, dysrhythmia—especially atrial fibrillation—venous thromboembolism, and respiratory failure. Sudden hypoxemia, unilateral change in breath sounds, hypotension, or rapidly increasing bloody drainage requires urgent bedside assessment and surgical escalation.

Provide ordered multimodal analgesia so the client can breathe deeply, cough, and move while monitoring for oversedation and hypoventilation. Assist with pulmonary hygiene, safe early ambulation, hydration and nutrition as ordered, and VTE prevention. Assess chest-drain function according to the actual operation and surgeon's orders. Do not apply a routine chest-tube rule to every pneumonectomy: drain use, clamping, suction, and positioning are procedure-specific and must be confirmed with the thoracic team. Never independently clamp or manipulate a drain to solve an alarm.

Recognize oncologic emergencies

Superior vena cava (SVC) syndrome may cause facial, neck, or arm swelling, distended upper-body veins, cough, dyspnea, headache, or worsening symptoms when supine. Stridor, confusion, or respiratory distress signals potential airway or cerebral compromise. Assess airway and oxygenation, elevate the head as tolerated, and urgently notify the treating team; definitive therapy depends on the cause.

Spinal cord compression may present as new severe back pain, weakness, sensory change, gait change, or bowel/bladder dysfunction. Treat a new neurologic deficit as time-sensitive and escalate promptly. SIADH, especially associated with SCLC, can produce low sodium, headache, confusion, seizures, or reduced consciousness; assess neurologic status and fluid and laboratory trends, institute seizure safety when indicated, and escalate severe symptoms. Hypercalcemia can cause dehydration, constipation, confusion, and weakness. Do not assume all confusion is anxiety or medication effect.

Monitor treatment toxicity and preserve quality of life

Chemotherapy can cause myelosuppression and infection risk; fever during neutropenia is urgent. Immunotherapy or thoracic radiation can cause pneumonitis: a new cough, dyspnea, hypoxemia, or fever during or after treatment warrants prompt evaluation rather than automatic attribution to infection or tumor progression. Targeted therapies have agent-specific adverse effects; verify the actual regimen and monitoring plan. Support nutrition, fatigue management, pain and dyspnea relief, smoking cessation, psychosocial needs, and palliative care when helpful. Palliative care may accompany disease-directed treatment and is not synonymous with abandoning treatment.

Apply clinical judgment

  1. Recognize cues: Identify eligibility and symptoms, oxygenation, bleeding, weight and function changes, procedure details, treatment regimen, and new neurologic or facial swelling findings.
  2. Analyze cues: Distinguish screening from diagnostic evaluation, expected recovery from deterioration, and cancer progression from infection or treatment toxicity.
  3. Prioritize hypotheses: Airway compromise, large-volume hemoptysis, unstable postoperative bleeding, pneumothorax, SVC syndrome with distress, cord compression, and symptomatic severe hyponatremia require immediate attention.
  4. Generate solutions: Support airway and breathing, call the appropriate rapid-response or specialty team, obtain ordered diagnostics, protect from falls or seizures, and prepare procedure-specific interventions.
  5. Take action: Reassess at the bedside, communicate precise trends and symptoms, follow postoperative and oncology protocols, and include the client in decisions.
  6. Evaluate outcomes: Trend oxygenation, work of breathing, hemodynamics, drain output, neurologic status, pain and function, treatment effects, and whether the agreed care goals are being met.

Clinical example

After lobectomy, a client reports increasing shortness of breath. The RN finds a falling oxygen saturation, tachycardia, new unilateral reduction in breath sounds, and increased work of breathing. The RN stays at the bedside, supports oxygenation as ordered, assesses the drain and incision without independently changing drain settings, calls for urgent surgical evaluation, and prepares for ordered imaging or rescue. Once stabilized, the team reviews pain control, pulmonary hygiene, mobility, and the cause of deterioration.

Screening eligibility, diagnostic workup, surgery, drain management, oncologic emergencies, and systemic-therapy monitoring require current recommendations, individualized orders, local protocols, and qualified clinical supervision. This lesson is not medical advice, clinical decision support, certification, continuing education, or an official USPSTF or NCI product.
